source.citation: BIPM. The International System of Units (SI Brochure), 9th edition, 2019: c = 299 792 458 m/s (exact, by definition).
Williams DR. Moon Fact Sheet. NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Goddard Space Flight Center (last updated 11 January 2024): semimajor axis 0.3844 x 10^6 km.
Williams DR. Moon Fact Sheet. NASA NSSDCA (last updated 11 January 2024): perigee 0.3633 x 10^6 km (mean perigee).
Williams DR. Moon Fact Sheet. NASA NSSDCA (last updated 11 January 2024): apogee 0.4055 x 10^6 km (mean apogee).

environments.label: ISS · low Earth orbit

source.rationale: Relay through geostationary TDRS satellites; the light path is a fraction of a second. 0-1 s is an envelope we chose, not a NASA figure, and excludes ground processing latency.

notes: NOAA S-scale flux is measured by GOES in geostationary orbit, outside the geomagnetic shielding the ISS orbit enjoys; NOAA's biological text is written for astronauts on EVA.
With the link up, Mission Control directs the response, including any sheltering; LANDFALL is the decision aid (meta.json escalation.autonomy).

environments.label: Cislunar space · spacecraft

source.rationale: Envelope for any point between Earth and 450,000 km (beyond the Moon's mean apogee of 405,500 km): 450,000 km / c = 1.50 s. Light time only; relay and processing latency are excluded.

notes: CRaTER dose is measured by LRO in lunar orbit; it stands in for deep-space dose and is not a dose inside a crewed vehicle.

environments.label: Lunar surface · base

source.arithmetic: one-way light time = Earth-Moon distance / c: 363,300 km / 299,792.458 km/s = 1.212 s (mean perigee); 384,400 km / c = 1.282 s (semimajor axis); 405,500 km / c = 1.353 s (mean apogee). Centre-to-centre distance; relay and processing latency excluded.

notes: No lunar-surface dosimetry snapshot is shipped; CRaTER (lunar orbit) is not a surface measurement, so dose_snapshot is null rather than borrowed.

The min/max above use the Moon's MEAN perigee and apogee. The JPL Horizons snapshot horizons_moon_comms gives the real 2026-2029 series (about 1.19 s to 1.36 s, since actual perigees come closer than the mean); prefer it for time-resolved values.

environments.label: Mars surface · base

source.arithmetic: one-way light time = Earth-Mars distance from the JPL Horizons ephemeris snapshot / c, per time step (computed by the ingest adapter, not here).

notes: noaa_scale_available is false on purpose: GOES measures near Earth, and during solar conjunction no NOAA alert reaches the crew. At Mars the SPE case reads an external space-weather monitor above the atmosphere, in Mars orbit, relayed to the habitat locally with no Earth link: the in-situ extravehicular monitoring [V2 6165] requires. The vehicle's radiation monitoring system raises the alarm ([V2 6164]); LANDFALL opens the health case.

Scenario assumption: the monitor's >=10 MeV reading is the GOES-7 October 1989 replay, with no radial-distance or atmospheric correction. The habitat dose rate shown at Mars is a separate simulated confirmation (an assumption, not a radiation-transport calculation).
The solar conjunction window is modelled from JPL Horizons geometry, its edges fitted to NASA's published command moratoria (RMS 0.79 d); it is not an announced window.
